correctness.rationale: For every prime p and exponent a>=2, proper unitary divisors are <=a/2; the normalized local sum is <=1+1/p with equality only a=2. Refined bounds R_2(a)<=39/32 (a>=4) and R_3(b)<=10/9 (b>=3, equality only b=3) are proved from explicit geometric-series envelopes. The unique squarefull core removes exponent-one factors; parity forces 2 in cores; the 39/20<2 bound forces the 2-adic exponent to 2 or 3 in three-prime cores. Divisibility by 3 or 5 and equality in the local bounds force exactly 2700 or 1800; the two-prime case is exactly 36. Reintroducing at most one squarefree prime completes the theorem. Exact standalone code verified 184320 triples and every integer <=350000 as independent consistency checks, not infinity proofs.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Neither a two-prime theorem nor a counting asymptotic logically implies a pointwise exhaustive three-prime classification. A classification of ordinary e-perfect integers could dominate the statement only when paired with an implication from e-unitary to e-perfect that is open in general; no such three-prime implication was found.

originality.rationale: Minculete--Toth (arXiv:0910.2798, full 2011 text, Section 4) introduces exponential-unitary perfect integers, names examples and poses the equivalence problem but provides no three-prime exhaustion. Published two-prime work closes only support size two; fixed-support asymptotics for ordinary exponential-perfect integers concern a different quantified property. OEIS A391281 lists sample powerful cores, not a proof that there are only two cores with three primes. A separate full elementary exclusion of all other three-prime cores is supplied. The 1978 e-perfect article is an inaccessible plausible source, retained as residual historical risk.

value.rationale: The original 2009/2011 paper explicitly asks whether an e-unitary perfect integer can fail to be e-perfect. A complete classification for omega(n)<=3 is the first natural support layer beyond the known two-prime theorem; it excludes all other powerful three-prime candidates, explains the special known examples, and raises the minimal support of any counterexample to at least four. This is an exact natural classification with an open-problem consequence, not a fabricated family or routine parameter instance.
